lessons.title: When to Plant: Timing with Rains and Temperature
lessons.body:
Planting at the right time is the single most important decision for your wheat and barley harvest. In most African smallholder regions, you want to sow when the rains have reliably started and the soil is moist to at least 15 cm deep. For wheat, the ideal soil temperature for germination is between 12Â°C and 25Â°C. Barley is tougher and can germinate at 5Â°C, but it still needs moisture. If you plant too early, seeds may rot in dry soil or be eaten by birds and insects. If you plant too late, the crop may hit drought or heat stress during flowering, cutting your yield by half or more.

In East Africa, for example, the long rains usually begin in late March to early April. Wheat should be planted within the first two weeks of steady rain. In the highlands of Ethiopia, barley is often planted in June or July with the main rains. In South Africa's winter rainfall region, plant wheat from mid-April to mid-June. For barley, you can plant two to three weeks earlier than wheat because it tolerates cold better. Always check with your local extension officer for the exact window in your area.

A simple test: dig a hole 15 cm deep. If the soil at the bottom is moist enough to form a ball when squeezed, and rain is forecast for the next few days, you can plant. If the soil is dry, wait. Do not plant into dry soil hoping for rainâit is a gamble that often fails. Also avoid planting right before a heavy storm, as seeds can wash away. The best time is when the soil is moist but not waterlogged.

Keep a record of your planting dates each season. After a few years, you will know the best week for your farm. Remember, a delay of just one week can reduce wheat yields by 10-20% in some areas. So prepare your land early and have your seed ready before the rains come.

lessons.title: Broadcasting vs. Row Planting: Pros and Cons
lessons.body:
Broadcasting means scattering seed by hand over the soil surface. It is fast and needs no special tools. A farmer can broadcast one hectare in about two hours. But it has big problems: seed falls unevenly, so some plants are crowded and others are far apart. You also need 20-30% more seed than row planting. Birds and rats eat more seed because it sits on top. Weeds grow easily because you cannot hoe between plants. And you cannot easily apply fertiliser or control weeds. Broadcasting is only recommended for very small plots or when you are short of labour and time.

Row planting means putting seeds in lines, usually 15-25 cm apart for wheat and barley. You can make rows with a hoe, a jab planter, or an ox-drawn drill. Row planting uses less seedâabout 100-120 kg per hectare for wheat instead of 150-180 kg for broadcasting. Plants get even sunlight, water, and nutrients. You can walk between rows to weed, top-dress fertiliser, and spray pests. Yields are typically 20-40% higher than broadcasting. The downside is that row planting takes more time and labour. With a hoe, one person can plant only 0.2-0.3 hectares per day. But the extra yield pays for the extra work.

For smallholders, a compromise is to broadcast then cover with a light harrow or rake. This improves seed-soil contact but still leaves uneven spacing. If you have oxen, an ox-drawn seed drill is bestâit opens a furrow, drops seed, and covers it in one pass. It can plant 1-2 hectares per day. If you have no oxen, a jab planter is a good manual tool. It makes a hole, drops a seed, and covers it. You can plant 0.5 hectares per day with a jab planter.

In short: broadcast only if you must, but aim for rows. Even simple rows made with a hoe will give you a better harvest. Start with a small area and compare. You will see the difference.

lessons.title: Using a Jab Planter or Ox-Drawn Seed Drill
lessons.body:
A jab planter is a hand-held tool that makes planting easy and precise. It has a metal spike that opens a hole in the soil, a seed hopper, and a mechanism that drops one or two seeds into the hole and covers it. You push it into the soil, squeeze the handle, and pull it out. The whole action takes about two seconds. With a jab planter, you can plant wheat or barley at the correct depth (3-5 cm) and spacing (15-20 cm between plants). You use less seedâabout 100 kg per hectareâand you do not have to bend down. A good jab planter costs $30-$60 and lasts several seasons. It is ideal for small plots up to 1 hectare.

To use a jab planter, first prepare a fine seedbed. Mark your rows with a string or a simple wooden marker. Set the planter to drop the right number of seeds. For wheat, one seed per hole is enough if spacing is 15 cm. For barley, one or two seeds. Walk backwards so you do not step on the planted rows. Keep the planter vertical and push it in to the correct depthâmost jab planters have a depth stop. After planting, you may need to lightly press the soil with your foot to ensure good seed contact.

An ox-drawn seed drill is a bigger investment but saves labour and time. It is a metal box with a seed hopper, tubes that drop seed into furrows, and a covering chain. Two oxen pull it. One person drives the oxen, another walks behind to check seed flow. A good drill can plant 1-2 hectares per day. It places seed at a consistent depth and spacing. You can also attach a fertiliser hopper to apply starter fertiliser at the same time. A new drill costs $300-$800, but you can share with neighbours or hire one from a cooperative. Many extension services offer drills for rent.

If you cannot afford a drill, consider a simple row marker and a hoe. But a jab planter is the best low-cost tool for smallholders. It pays for itself in one or two seasons through saved seed and higher yields.

lessons.title: Correct Seed Rate and Spacing for Wheat and Barley
lessons.body:
Seed rate is the amount of seed you plant per hectare. If you plant too little, you get fewer plants and lower yield. If you plant too much, plants compete for water and nutrients, and you waste money on seed. For wheat, the recommended seed rate for smallholders is 100-120 kg per hectare. For barley, it is 80-100 kg per hectare. These rates assume good seed with at least 85% germination. If your seed is older or poor quality, increase the rate by 10-20%. For broadcasting, you need 150-180 kg per hectare for wheat and 120-150 kg for barley because not all seed will establish.

Spacing is the distance between plants and between rows. For wheat, aim for 15-20 cm between rows and 5-10 cm between plants within the row. That gives about 200-300 plants per square metre. For barley, rows can be 15-25 cm apart, with 5-8 cm between plants. Barley tillers more than wheat, so it can be a bit thinner. If you are using a jab planter, drop one seed every 15 cm in the row. If you are using a drill, set the seed metering to the correct rate. A simple way to check: plant a small area, then count the seeds in one square metre. You should find 200-300 seeds for wheat, 150-250 for barley.

Many farmers in Africa plant too thickly because they fear poor germination. But thick planting leads to weak stems, more disease, and smaller heads. It also uses more water. On the other hand, too thin planting lets weeds take over. The best approach is to test your seed germination before planting. Take 100 seeds, put them in a moist cloth for 5 days, and count how many sprout. If 85 or more sprout, use the normal rate. If fewer, increase the rate.

Also consider row spacing for weeding. Wider rows (25-30 cm) allow you to use a hoe or ox-drawn cultivator between rows. Narrow rows (15 cm) shade the soil and suppress weeds, but you cannot easily weed. For smallholders with limited labour, 20-25 cm rows are a good compromise. Always calibrate your planter or drill before planting the whole field. A small mistake in seed rate can cost you a lot of yield.

lessons.title: Planting Depth: Why 3-5 cm Matters
lessons.body:
Planting depth is the distance from the soil surface to the seed. For wheat and barley, the ideal depth is 3-5 cm. If you plant too shallow (less than 2 cm), the seed may dry out before it sprouts, or birds will eat it. The roots may also be exposed. If you plant too deep (more than 6 cm), the seedling uses all its energy to push through the soil and may die before it reaches sunlight. Deep planting also makes the plant more vulnerable to soil-borne diseases. A seed planted at 3-5 cm has enough moisture and warmth to germinate quickly and emerge strongly.

How do you get the right depth? First, prepare a fine seedbed. Large clods and rocks make depth uneven. If you are using a jab planter, set the depth stop to 4 cm. Most jab planters have a metal plate that you can adjust. Push the planter into the soil until the plate touches the surface. That puts the seed at the right depth. If you are using a hoe, make a furrow 4-5 cm deep. You can check by putting a stick in the furrow and marking the soil level. Drop the seed, then cover with 2-3 cm of soil. Do not cover too deep.

For an ox-drawn drill, adjust the depth wheels or the tension on the furrow openers. The drill should place seed at 3-5 cm. After planting, check a few spots by digging carefully with your hands. If you find seeds at 2 cm or 7 cm, adjust the drill. Also, soil type matters. In sandy soil, plant a bit deeper (5 cm) because it dries out faster. In clay soil, plant at 3-4 cm because it holds moisture longer and can crust over. If the soil is very dry on top, you may need to plant deeper to reach moisture, but never deeper than 6 cm.

After planting, press the soil lightly with a roller or your foot. This improves seed-soil contact and helps the seed absorb water. But do not compact the soil too much. A good rule: if you can see the seed after a light rain, it was too shallow. If the seedlings take more than 10 days to emerge, they may be too deep. Check and adjust next time. Correct depth is a simple thing that makes a big difference.

lessons.title: Intercropping with Legumes for Soil Health
lessons.body:
Intercropping means growing two or more crops together in the same field. For wheat and barley, the best partners are legumes like faba beans, field peas, lentils, or chickpeas. Legumes pull nitrogen from the air and put it into the soil. This reduces your need for fertiliser and improves soil health. In Africa, many smallholders already intercrop maize with beans. You can do the same with wheat or barley. The legume also provides ground cover, which reduces weeds and erosion. And you get a second crop to eat or sell.

How to intercrop? One simple method is to plant one row of wheat or barley, then one row of legumes. For example, plant wheat at 20 cm row spacing, and after every 4 rows of wheat, plant 1 row of faba beans. Or you can mix seed and broadcast both together, but row intercropping is better for management. The legume should be planted at the same time as the cereal or slightly later. For faba beans, use 50-60 kg seed per hectare. For field peas, 40-50 kg per hectare. Do not plant the legume too thickly, or it will compete with the cereal.

Intercropping has many benefits. The legume fixes 20-60 kg of nitrogen per hectare, which can increase wheat yield by 10-20% in the next season. The legume also breaks disease cycles. For example, wheat rust does not affect faba beans. The cereal stems support the legume, and the legume covers the soil. But there are challenges. You need to manage two crops. If you use a herbicide, it may kill the legume. So you must weed by hand or use selective herbicides. Also, the legume may attract pests that also attack wheat, like aphids. Monitor your field regularly.

A good rotation is to intercrop this season, then next season plant the legume as a sole crop, then wheat. This builds soil fertility. In Ethiopia, farmers often intercrop barley with faba beans and get good results. In Kenya, wheat with field peas is common. Start with a small plot. If it works, expand. Intercropping is a low-cost way to improve your soil and your harvest.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Planting Techniques for Smallholder Wheat & Barley Farms

This practical reference consolidates the six core lessons in this module into a single field-ready guide. It is written for smallholder farmers, extension officers, and agripreneurs across the Ethiopian Highlands, Kenya's Rift Valley, Tanzania's Southern Highlands, and similar cereal zones where wheat and barley are both food and cash crops. The goal is business-first: every decision here â timing, method, seed rate, depth, intercropping â should translate into higher yield per hectare, lower input cost, or better resilience against drought and disease. In smallholder systems, a 10â20% gain in establishment efficiency often means the difference between a subsistence harvest and a marketable surplus.

1. When to Plant: Timing with Rains and Temperature

Planting date is the single most powerful yield lever in rainfed smallholder systems. Wheat and barley germinate reliably when soil temperature is between 12 Â°C and 25 Â°C and when 25â40 mm of rain has fallen to wet the seedbed. In Ethiopia's Arsi and Bale zones, the optimum window is late June to mid-July; in Kenya's Narok and Uasin Gishu counties, it is late March to mid-April for the long-rains crop. Barley tolerates slightly cooler soils than wheat and can be planted 7â10 days earlier. Late planting pushes grain fill into heat stress and terminal drought, cutting yields by 30â50%.

2. Broadcasting vs. Row Planting

Broadcasting is fast and needs little equipment, but it wastes seed (30â50% more seed per hectare), produces uneven depth, and makes weeding and fertiliser placement difficult. Row planting â whether by hand hoe, jab planter, or ox-drawn drill â gives uniform depth, easier weeding, and typically 15â25% higher yields for the same seed. For a market-oriented smallholder, the extra labour of row planting is repaid by better grain quality and easier harvest.

3. Using a Jab Planter or Ox-Drawn Seed Drill

The jab planter is the cheapest entry into precision planting: one person can plant 0.3â0.5 ha per day with consistent depth and spacing. Ox-drawn seed drills (such as the Ethiopian Bereket or the CIMMYT-designed zero-till drill) cover 1â2 ha per day, place seed and fertiliser together, and reduce labour by 40â60%. For smallholders renting oxen, a drill also improves timeliness â critical when the rains start late.

4. Correct Seed Rate and Spacing

Seed rate depends on variety, seed size, and germination percentage. Adjust upward if germination is below 90%. Row spacing of 20â25 cm is standard for smallholder wheat and barley; closer rows suppress weeds but increase seed cost.

Table 1: Recommended Seed Rate and Spacing for Smallholder Wheat & Barley
Crop Seed Rate (kg/ha) Row Spacing (cm) Target Plant Population (plants/mÂ²) Typical Yield Potential (t/ha)
Bread wheat (rainfed)100â15020â25250â3002.5â4.5
Durum wheat (rainfed)110â16020â25250â3002.0â4.0
Barley (rainfed)80â12020â25250â3502.0â4.0
Barley (irrigated)100â14018â22300â3504.0â6.0

Source: Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR), Crop Production Recommendations (2021); FAO, Wheat and Barley Production Guide for Eastern Africa (2019).

5. Planting Depth: Why 3â5 cm Matters

Too shallow (<2 cm) and seed dries out or is eaten by birds; too deep (>6 cm) and the seedling exhausts its reserves before reaching light. The 3â5 cm band balances moisture access with emergence vigour. On heavy clay soils, aim for the shallower end (3 cm); on sandy soils, 4â5 cm. In dry seedbeds, plant deeper; in wet seedbeds, shallower.

6. Intercropping with Legumes for Soil Health

Intercropping wheat or barley with faba bean, field pea, or chickpea fixes 20â60 kg N/ha, breaks disease cycles, and improves soil structure. On smallholder farms, a 1:1 or 2:1 cereal-legume row ratio is practical. The legume also provides a second income stream (grain or fodder) and reduces risk if the cereal fails.

Table 2: Intercropping Options for Wheat & Barley in Eastern Africa
Legume Partner Row Ratio (Cereal:Legume) N Fixed (kg/ha) Extra Benefit
Faba bean2:140â60High-protein fodder
Field pea2:125â40Early maturity, good for short rains
Chickpea1:120â35Drought tolerance, marketable grain
Lentil1:115â30High-value pulse for local markets

Source: ICARDA, Legume-Cereal Intercropping in Dry Areas (2020); CIMMYT, Sustainable Intensification for Smallholders (2022).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Seed Treatment and Fertiliser Handling

Treated seed (fungicide/insecticide-coated) is toxic to humans and livestock. Never eat, feed to animals, or use treated seed for food. Store treated seed in labelled, sealed containers away from children and food. Wear gloves and a nose mask when handling treated seed or applying fertiliser. Wash hands and tools after planting. Do not plant treated seed within 24 hours of heavy rain to avoid runoff contamination of water sources.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm soil temperature is 12â25 Â°C and 25â40 mm rain has fallen before planting.
  • â Test seed germination; increase seed rate if germination is below 90%.
  • â Choose row planting over broadcasting for better depth control and weeding.
  • â Calibrate jab planter or ox-drawn drill before the first pass in the field.
  • â Set seed depth at 3â5 cm; shallower on clay, deeper on sand.
  • â Use 100â150 kg/ha wheat or 80â120 kg/ha barley at 20â25 cm row spacing.
  • â Intercrop with faba bean, field pea, or chickpea at 2:1 or 1:1 row ratio.
  • â Wear gloves and mask when handling treated seed or fertiliser; store safely.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course on Wheat & Barley Farming. It is designed for smallholder farmers and agripreneurs seeking to increase yield, reduce cost, and build resilient cereal-legume systems across Eastern and Southern Africa.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil temperature range for wheat germination?
quiz.explanation: Wheat germinates best when soil temperature is between 12Â°C and 25Â°C.

quiz.q: Which crop can be planted two to three weeks earlier than wheat because it tolerates cold better?
quiz.explanation: Barley is more cold-tolerant than wheat and can be planted earlier.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to check if soil is moist enough for planting?
options: A) Dig a hole 15 cm deep and squeeze the soil
quiz.explanation: If soil at 15 cm depth forms a ball when squeezed, it has enough moisture.

quiz.q: How much can a delay of one week reduce wheat yields in some areas?
quiz.explanation: Late planting can reduce wheat yields by 10-20% per week of delay.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of broadcasting seed?
quiz.explanation: Broadcasting leads to uneven seed distribution, causing crowded and sparse areas.

quiz.q: How much more seed does broadcasting require compared to row planting?
quiz.explanation: Broadcasting typically needs 20-30% more seed than row planting.

quiz.q: What is a typical yield advantage of row planting over broadcasting?
quiz.explanation: Row planting usually gives 20-40% higher yields than broadcasting.

quiz.q: How many hectares can one person plant per day with a hoe in rows?
quiz.explanation: Manual row planting with a hoe covers only 0.2-0.3 hectares per day.

quiz.q: What is a jab planter?
options: A) A hand-held tool that makes a hole and drops seed
quiz.explanation: A jab planter is a manual tool that opens a hole, drops seed, and covers it.

quiz.q: How many hectares can a jab planter cover per day?
quiz.explanation: A jab planter can plant about 0.5 hectares per day.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of an ox-drawn seed drill?
options: B) It plants at consistent depth and spacing
quiz.explanation: A seed drill places seed at uniform depth and spacing, improving establishment.

quiz.q: What should you do after planting with a jab planter to improve seed contact?
options: B) Press the soil lightly with your foot
quiz.explanation: Lightly pressing the soil ensures good seed-to-soil contact for germination.

quiz.q: What is the recommended seed rate for wheat in smallholder systems?
quiz.explanation: The recommended wheat seed rate is 100-120 kg per hectare for row planting.

quiz.q: What is the recommended seed rate for barley?
quiz.explanation: Barley seed rate is 80-100 kg per hectare for row planting.

quiz.q: If your seed has only 70% germination, what should you do?
quiz.explanation: Poor germination requires a higher seed rate to achieve target plant population.

quiz.q: What is the ideal row spacing for wheat to allow weeding?
quiz.explanation: Wider rows of 25-30 cm allow easy hoeing or ox-cultivation between rows.

quiz.q: How many wheat plants per square metre should you aim for?
quiz.explanation: A good wheat stand is about 200-300 plants per square metre.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to test seed germination before planting?
options: B) Put 100 seeds in a moist cloth for 5 days
C) Plant them in the field
D) Look at the seed color
quiz.explanation: A moist cloth test shows the percentage of seeds that sprout.

quiz.q: What is the ideal planting depth for wheat and barley?
quiz.explanation: Seeds planted at 3-5 cm have enough moisture and warmth for good emergence.

quiz.q: What happens if you plant wheat too shallow (less than 2 cm)?
options: A) Seed may dry out or be eaten by birds
quiz.explanation: Shallow planting exposes seed to drying and bird damage.

quiz.q: What happens if you plant wheat too deep (more than 6 cm)?
options: A) Seedling uses too much energy to emerge
quiz.explanation: Deep planting exhausts seedling reserves before it reaches sunlight.

quiz.q: In sandy soil, at what depth should you plant wheat?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soil dries faster, so plant slightly deeper at 5 cm.

quiz.q: How can you check if your drill is planting at the right depth?
options: A) Dig a few spots with your hands
quiz.explanation: Digging carefully after planting reveals actual seed depth.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of intercropping wheat with legumes?
quiz.explanation: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for the cereal.

quiz.q: Which legume is commonly intercropped with wheat or barley in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Faba beans, field peas, and lentils are common cool-season legumes for intercropping.

quiz.q: How much nitrogen can legumes fix per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Legumes can fix 20-60 kg of nitrogen per hectare, benefiting the next crop.

quiz.q: What is a challenge of intercropping wheat with legumes?
options: A) Herbicides may kill the legume
B) Legumes fix too much nitrogen
quiz.explanation: Many herbicides are selective and can harm broadleaf legumes.

quiz.q: What is a good intercropping pattern for wheat and faba beans?
options: D) Plant beans after wheat harvest
quiz.explanation: A 4:1 row ratio balances competition and nitrogen fixation.

quiz.q: What should you do if you use a herbicide in an intercrop?
options: A) Use a selective herbicide safe for legumes
quiz.explanation: Selective herbicides that do not harm legumes are essential for intercropping.

quiz.q: What is a recommended rotation after intercropping wheat with legumes?
options: B) Plant legume as sole crop
quiz.explanation: Following intercropping with a sole legume crop builds soil nitrogen further.
